title: Level 3 (Advanced) - D-6
notes:
West leads the ♠5 against 3NT. It seems natural to play a low spade from the dummy in order to guarantee 3 spade tricks, but if South does so he will be sorry. If East has the ♠Q he will force out South's ♠A.

When the ♣Q does not drop under the ♣A and ♣K, South lacks the 2 hand entries required to set up and run the clubs.

South can avoid this problem by winning West's spade opening lead with dummy's ♠K. South does not need 3 spade tricks, but he does need 2 entries to his hand in order to enjoy his long club suit. When the ♣A and ♣K are cashed and the ♣Q has not dropped, South can cross to his hand in spades and force out the ♣Q. The ♦A will act as an entry to South's remaining club winners. Provided that the defense cannot win 4 spade tricks, the contract is assured.

It is a near certainty that spades are no worse than 5-3 given the opening lead of the ♠5. Players generally lead 4th best from a long suit and the ♠4 is the only outstanding spade lower than the ♠5. Therefore, West was dealt no more than 5 spades and South can safely use the ♠A as his first hand entry. It would not be safe to cross the first time in diamonds as it is possible that one of the defenders (most likely East) was dealt a 5-card diamond suit.
